video_caption: The video opens with a dark blue slide titled "Cell Membrane or Plasma Membrane" in white text at the top. Below the title, it says "Photo: National Institute of Standards and Technology" (Photo: National Institute of Standards and Technology). On the right side, an animated illustration shows a cross-section of a cell membrane, depicting a bilayer of yellowish-green molecules, with "Cell Exterior" written above it and "Cell Interior" below. A yellow-green L-shaped line frames the top-left corner of the slide. At the 0:02 mark, the slide transitions to a similar layout, retaining the main title "Cell Membrane or Plasma Membrane," but the photo credit changes to "Photo credit: Encyclopedia Britannica" (Photo credit: Encyclopedia Britannica). On the left, a bulleted list appears with five points: "Separates cell's interior from outside," "Acts as a 'border' – allowing selective cargo to pass," "Analogous to border control – where they wouldn't allow anyone to pass without checks," "Transports nutrients and expels cell's waste," and "Different types of membranes in different cells." The image on the right also changes to a more intricate diagram of a cell membrane, showcasing various components such as proteins, cholesterol, and sugar chains embedded within the lipid bilayer, and is labeled with terms like "outer face," "inner face," "hydrophilic (polar) head," "hydrophobic (nonpolar) fatty acyl tail," "sugar side chain," "cholesterol," "integral (intrinsic) protein," and "peripheral (extrinsic) protein," along with a copyright notice "© 2001 Encyclopedia Britannica, Inc." The yellow-green L-shaped line remains, framing the top-left of the slide.

The video displays a static presentation slide with a dark blue background and a light blue horizontal bar at the top left. The main title of the slide is "Cell Membrane or Plasma Membrane" in white text. Below the title, there are five bullet points, also in white text, describing the functions of the cell membrane: "Separates cell's interior from outside", "Acts as a 'border' – allowing selective cargo to pass", "Analogous to border control – where they wouldn’t allow anyone to pass without checks", "Transports nutrients and expels cell’s waste", and "Different types of membranes in different cells". Below these points, in smaller white text, is "Photo credit: Encyclopedia Britannica". On the right side of the slide is a detailed diagram of a cell membrane, illustrating its bilayer structure. Various components are labeled in the diagram, including "hydrophilic head of phospholipid", "hydrophobic tail of phospholipid", "cholesterol", "integral (intrinsic) protein", "peripheral (extrinsic) protein", and "sugar side chain". The diagram also indicates the "outer face" and "inner face" of the membrane.

The video segment presents a series of educational slides about the cell membrane, featuring a male voice narrating the information. Each slide has a dark blue background with white text and a diagram.

From 00:00 to 00:05, the slide is titled "Cell Membrane or Plasma Membrane" and lists bullet points describing its functions: "Separates cell's interior from outside", "Acts as a 'border' – allowing selective cargo to pass", "Analogous to border control – where they wouldn't allow anyone to pass without checks", "Transports nutrients and expels cell's waste", and "Different types of membranes in different cells". Below the bullet points, "Photo credit: Encyclopedia Britannica" is visible. On the right side, a diagram illustrates a simplified cell membrane, showing a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins and associated molecules, labeled with "outer face" and "inner face". The narrator begins by mentioning different types of cell membranes and states a focus on a general model.

At 00:05, the slide transitions to a new one titled "Structure of Cell Membrane". The bullet points detail its composition: "Made up of both lipids and proteins", "Fundamentally—it is phospholipid bilayer", "The outer part - phosphatidylcholine, sphingomyelin, & glycolipids", "Inner part - phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine, & phosphatidylinositol", and "Cholesterol—in both sides." The photo credit "Photo: © 2000, Geoffrey M Cooper." is at the bottom left. The diagram on the right is more detailed, showcasing the phospholipid bilayer with specific phospholipid types labeled for both the "Outside of cell" and "Cytosol" sides, along with cholesterol molecules. The narrator elaborates on these components, occasionally pausing or rephrasing for pronunciation, and emphasizes the membrane's role as a "strong wall".

At 00:57, the slide changes again to one titled "Membrane Proteins". The bullet points highlight their role: "Lipids - fundamental element of the membrane", "Proteins - carry out membrane functions", "Most plasma membrane - 50% protein and 50% lipid by weight", "Carbohydrate portion - 5% to 10%", "Jonathan Singer and Garth Nicolson - proposed Fluid Mosaic model", and "Now accepted as basic model of all biological membrane". The same photo credit from the previous slide is present. The accompanying diagram displays various integral and peripheral membrane proteins embedded in or attached to the phospholipid bilayer, some with attached carbohydrate chains. The narrator prompts to discuss membrane proteins.

The video segment displays a presentation slide with a dark blue background, titled "Membrane Proteins" in white text at the top left. Below the title, a series of bullet points explain key aspects of membrane proteins: "Lipids - fundamental element of the membrane," "Proteins - carry out membrane functions," "Most plasma membrane - 50% protein and 50% lipid by weight," "Carbohydrate portion - 5% to 10%," "Jonathan Singer and Garth Nicolson - proposed Fluid Mosaic model," and "Now accepted as basic model of all biological membrane." To the right of the text, an illustrative diagram depicts the fluid mosaic model of a cell membrane. It shows a double layer of yellow phospholipid molecules forming the membrane, with various irregularly shaped proteins (colored green, light blue, purple, and red) embedded within or attached to it. Some proteins are labeled as "integral membrane protein" and "peripheral membrane protein," and carbohydrate chains are seen extending from proteins and lipids on the outer surface, labeled "Carbohydrate." At the bottom left, there's a photo credit: "Photo: © 2000, Geoffrey M Cooper." The speaker is heard explaining the content of the slide, elaborating on lipids, proteins, and the composition of the plasma membrane.

The video displays two distinct slides, each featuring a detailed diagram of a cell membrane on the right side against a dark blue background, with bulleted text on the left. The first slide, presented from 0:00 to 0:11, is titled "Membrane Proteins." Its bullet points state that lipids are fundamental elements, proteins carry out membrane functions and constitute 50% of most plasma membranes by weight, the carbohydrate portion is 5% to 10%, Jonathan Singer and Garth Nicolson proposed the Fluid Mosaic Model, and this model is now accepted as the basic model for all biological membranes. The diagram shows a lipid bilayer (yellow phospholipids) with various proteins (green, red, pink, light blue, purple) either embedded within it (integral membrane proteins) or attached to its surface (peripheral membrane proteins), some proteins and lipids are also shown with attached carbohydrate chains on the exterior. At 0:11, the slide transitions to the second slide, titled "Fluid Mosaic Model," which retains the same cell membrane diagram. The bullet points on this slide provide further details: integral membrane proteins are inserted inside the membrane, peripheral proteins are indirectly bound by protein-protein interaction, integral proteins are transmembrane proteins with portions exposed on both sides of the membrane, and portions of proteins outside the membrane are glycosylated. Both slides include a footer: "Photo: © 2000, Geoffrey M Cooper."

The video displays a presentation slide with a blue background, titled "Fluid Mosaic Model." On the left, there are four bullet points describing different types of membrane proteins: "Integral membrane proteins - inserted inside the membrane," "Peripheral proteins - indirectly bound to the membrane by protein-protein interaction," "Integral proteins - transmembrane proteins w/portion exposed on both sides of membrane," and "Portion of proteins outside membrane - glycosylated." On the right, a detailed colorful diagram illustrates the fluid mosaic model of a cell membrane. It shows a yellow phospholipid bilayer embedded with various integral membrane proteins, colored purple, green, blue, pink, orange, and red, some of which are transmembrane. Peripheral membrane proteins, colored yellow and brown, are shown on the surface. Carbohydrate chains, represented by blue and pink stick figures, are attached to some proteins and lipids on the outer surface, labeled "Carbohydrate." Labels within the diagram also point to "integral membrane protein" and "peripheral membrane protein." Below the image, the credit reads, "Photo: © 2000, Geoffrey M Cooper." The slide remains static throughout the segment.

The video displays a blue-background slide titled "Fluid Mosaic Model." On the left side, bullet points describe different types of membrane proteins: "Integral membrane proteins - inserted inside the membrane," "Peripheral proteins - indirectly bound to the membrane by protein-protein interaction," "Integral proteins - transmembrane proteins w/portion exposed on both sides of membrane," and "Portion of proteins outside membrane - glycosylated." A copyright note, "Photo: © 2000, Geoffrey M Cooper," is at the bottom. On the right, a detailed diagram illustrates the fluid mosaic model of a cell membrane, featuring a lipid bilayer with various integral (blue, purple, red, green, yellow) and peripheral (yellow, green) proteins embedded and attached. Carbohydrate chains (grey) are visible on the exterior of some proteins. The speaker's cursor points to a blue integral membrane protein with attached carbohydrates while explaining glycosylation (00:09-00:13).

At 00:14, the slide transitions to new bullet points on the left, continuing the "Fluid Mosaic Model" theme. These points detail the phospholipid molecule: "The main part of membrane - amphiphilic phospholipid molecules," "Amphiphilic - both water hating and water loving molecules," "Phospholipid - made of hydrophilic head, & two hydrophobic tails," "Hydrophilic head - phosphate grp attached to glycerol molecule," and "Hydrophobic tails - saturated and unsaturated fatty acid chain." A reference note at the bottom states, "Ref: “Fluid Mosaic Model” by LibreTexts is licensed under notset" (meaning "no license set"). On the right, a simplified diagram of a single phospholipid molecule is shown, consisting of a red circular "Hydrophilic head" (containing "Phosphate" and "Glycerol" components) and two yellow "Hydrophobic tails" extending downwards, labeled "Saturated fatty acid" and "Unsaturated fatty acid."

The video segment displays a presentation slide titled "Fluid Mosaic Model" at the top left. On the left side of the slide, there are bullet points detailing aspects of the fluid mosaic model, including: "The main part of membrane - amphiphilic phospholipid molecules," "Amphiphilic - both water hating and water loving molecules," "Phospholipid - made of hydrophilic head, & two hydrophobic tails," "Hydrophilic head - phosphate grp attached to glycerol molecule," and "Hydrophobic tails- saturated and unsaturated fatty acid chain." Below these points, a reference note reads, "Ref: “Fluid Mosaic Model” by LibreTexts is licensed under notset." On the right side of the slide, there is a diagram of a single phospholipid molecule. This diagram shows a red, circular "Hydrophilic head" at the top, which contains chemical structures labeled "Phosphate" and "Glycerol." Extending from the head are two yellow, wavy "Hydrophobic tails," one straight and labeled "Saturated fatty acid," and the other bent and labeled "Unsaturated fatty acid." A white mouse cursor appears on the diagram at 0:05, first hovering near the left hydrophobic tail, then moving to the red hydrophilic head, and finally pointing to the "Phosphate" label within the head by 0:08.

The video segment displays two educational slides on a blue background, accompanied by a voice-over. The first slide, titled "Fluid Mosaic Model," presents bullet points defining integral proteins as major components of the plasma membrane (PM), completely embedded within it, and interacting with the hydrophobic region of phospholipids. It notes that some proteins are composed of multiple segments and are extensively folded, specifically mentioning integral membrane proteins with one or more alpha-helices (labeled 1 and 2 in the accompanying diagram) or beta-sheets (labeled 3 in the diagram) that span the PM. The diagram on the right illustrates these protein types embedded in a light yellow horizontal band representing the membrane; protein 1 shows a single alpha-helix, protein 2 multiple alpha-helices, and the unlabeled third protein shows a beta-barrel structure. A mouse cursor points to these structures as the speaker elaborates. At 01:08, the slide transitions to "Plasma Membrane & Disease," listing bullet points about membrane composition, consequences of membrane damage, receptor-related diseases (hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes & obesity, Grave's disease), and cell structural instability like RBC abnormalities and altered transport systems, as seen in cystic fibrosis. The accompanying image, titled "Cystic Fibrosis," shows a comparison between a healthy trachea (with a clear lumen) and a cystic fibrosis trachea (with a lumen blocked by mucus), alongside a general diagram of the lungs and trachea.

The video segment displays a blue presentation slide titled "Plasma Membrane & Disease". On the left side of the slide, there are five bullet points. The first states, "Membrane composed of – array of lipids and proteins". The second reads, "Any damage to the membrane integrity – leads to consequences". The third bullet point lists "Some receptors related diseases – hypercholesterolaemia, some forms of diabetes & obesity, Grave’s disease". The fourth point describes "Cell structural instability – RBC abnormalities and altered transport system, as in cystic fibrosis." The final bullet point provides an image reference link: "https://www.labiotech.eu/trends-news/cystic-fibrosis-gen e-therapy/". On the right side of the slide, an illustration labeled "Cystic Fibrosis" is shown. This illustration contains two sets of images: one labeled "Healthy" and the other "Cystic Fibrosis." Both sets include an anatomical drawing of the lungs and a cross-section of a trachea. In the "Healthy" trachea cross-section, the lumen is clear. In contrast, the "Cystic Fibrosis" trachea cross-section shows a significant green mass labeled "Mucus" obstructing the lumen. No people are visible in the video, but a voice can be heard discussing the content of the slide, specifically mentioning the composition of the membrane and the consequences of its damage.

The video segment displays a dark blue presentation slide titled "Plasma Membrane & Disease." On the left, a bulleted list outlines points about membrane composition, consequences of membrane damage, related diseases (hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes, obesity, Grave's disease), and cell structural instability (RBC abnormalities and altered transport system, as in cystic fibrosis). Below the list, an image reference is provided: "Img ref: https://www.labiotech.eu/trends-news/cystic-fibrosis-gene-therapy/". On the right side of the slide, an illustration titled "Cystic Fibrosis" depicts a pair of lungs and two cross-sections of a trachea. One tracheal cross-section is labeled "Healthy" with a clear lumen, while the other is labeled "Cystic Fibrosis" and shows mucus buildup in the lumen. The image also labels "Trachea," "Lung," "Lumen," and "Smooth muscle." The slide remains static throughout the segment.

A dark blue presentation slide titled "Plasma Membrane & Disease" in white text is displayed. On the left side, there are bullet points in white text outlining aspects of the plasma membrane and its relation to diseases. The first bullet states, "Membrane composed of – array of lipids and proteins," followed by "Any damage to the membrane integrity – leads to consequences." The third point lists "Some receptors related diseases – hypercholesterolaemia, some forms of diabetes & obesity, Grave’s disease." The fourth bullet mentions "Cell structural instability – RBC abnormalities and altered transport system, as in cystic fibrosis." Below these points, an image reference is provided: "Img ref: https://www.labiotech.eu/trends-news/cystic-fibrosis-gen-e-therapy/". On the right side of the slide, an illustration titled "Cystic Fibrosis" shows a simplified diagram of human lungs connected to a trachea. To the right of the lungs, two circular cross-sections of the trachea are depicted. The top circle, labeled "Healthy," shows a clear airway (lumen). The bottom circle, labeled "Cystic Fibrosis," illustrates the airway filled with a thick green substance, labeled "Mucus," indicating a blocked or constricted passage.

The video opens with a static slide titled "Plasma Membrane & Disease" on a dark blue background, featuring bullet points and an image illustrating "Cystic Fibrosis." The bullet points describe the membrane's composition of lipids and proteins, the consequences of damage to its integrity, receptor-related diseases such as hypercholesterolemia, diabetes, obesity, and Grave's disease, and cell structural instability like RBC abnormalities and altered transport systems in cystic fibrosis. To the right, an image shows a "Healthy" trachea with a clear lumen and a "Cystic Fibrosis" trachea with a constricted lumen filled with mucus, with the image reference provided below. The speaker emphasizes the need to maintain the plasma membrane's integrity. At 00:11, the slide transitions to a dark blue background displaying white text that reads: "Thank you once again! Any questions, please comment or write to me deepesh.soni@mail.ru." (Thank you once again! Any questions, please comment or write to me deepesh.soni@mail.ru). The speaker concludes the presentation, thanks the audience, invites questions via comments or email, and announces that the next presentation will be about the cytoskeleton.
